text: Sir William Beechey RA (12 December 1753 – 28 January 1839) was a British portraitist active during the golden age of British painting. Born in Burford, Oxfordshire, on 12 December 1753, he was the son of William Beechey, a solicitor, and Hannah Read. Both parents died in the early 1760s, and he and his siblings were raised by his uncle Samuel, a solicitor in Chipping Norton. Samuel intended for William to follow a legal career, and at an appropriate age, he was apprenticed as a clerk to a conveyancer near Stow-on-the-Wold. However, as recorded in The Monthly Mirror in July 1798, he was "Early foredoomed his [uncle's] soul to cross/ And paint a picture where he should engross." Beechey entered the Royal Academy Schools in 1772, where he is believed to have studied under Johan Zoffany. He first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1776, with his earliest surviving works being small-scale full-length and conversation pieces reminiscent of Zoffany. In 1782, he moved to Norwich, where he received commissions such as a portrait of John Wodehouse and a series of civic portraits for St. Andrew's Hall. By 1787, he had returned to London, and in 1789, he exhibited a celebrated portrait of John Douglas, Bishop of Carlisle (now in Lambeth Palace). His early career featured portraits in the restrained style of Joshua Reynolds. Beechey's style aligned well with the royal family's tastes, and in 1793, he was commissioned to paint a full-length portrait of Queen Charlotte and appointed her official portrait painter. That same year, he was elected an associate member of the Royal Academy. Following this appointment, royal commissions increased significantly, and in 1797 he exhibited six royal portraits. In 1798, he was elected a full member of the Royal Academy and painted George III and the Prince of Wales Reviewing Troops for the Academy's exhibition—an enormous composition depicting the King, the Prince of Wales, and staff officers on horseback at an imagined cavalry review in Hyde Park. The King was pleased with the painting and awarded Beechey a knighthood. Joseph Farington's Diaries document Beechey's relationships with the royal family, including a temporary fall from favour in 1804, which Farington attributed to George III's mental condition. Beechey's portraits at the turn of the century are regarded as his most colourful and lively, reflecting the flamboyant and free techniques of his younger rivals, John Hoppner and Sir Thomas Lawrence. Royal patronage resumed around 1813 when Beechey was appointed portrait painter to Prince William Frederick, Duke of Gloucester and Edinburgh, culminating in his appointment in 1830 as principal portrait painter to William IV. In 1830, he stood for election as President of the Royal Academy following Thomas Lawrence's death, finishing second to Martin Archer Shee. In 1836, Beechey retired to Hampstead, and on 9–11 June of that year, the contents of his studio and collection were sold at Christie's. Despite being capable of impetuousness and irascibility, Beechey was known for his generosity to students, particularly supporting the young John Constable. Over a half-century-long career, he painted many leading figures of his time, including Capt. Jack Aubrey, whose portrait—showing him in Royal Navy uniform with the insignia of the Order of the Bath—was described by Patrick O'Brian in his 1978 novel Desolation Island as having hung in Aubrey's home, Ashgrove Cottage. His first marriage was to Mary Ann Jones (c. 1760–1793) in 1772 (some sources state 1778); they had a son, British painter and Egyptologist Henry William Beechey (1788–1862). After Mary Ann's death, he married the successful miniature painter Anne Phyllis Jessop (1764–1833) in 1793; they had several children, including Royal Navy captain, geographer, and politician Frederick William Beechey (1796–1856); painter George Duncan Beechey (1798–1852); clergyman St. Vincent Beechey (1806–1899); and painter and admiral Richard Brydges Beechey (1808–1895). Beechey's Portrait of James Watt sold for £153,440 at Sotheby's on 20 March 2003; his Portrait of Mirza Abu'l Hassan Khan, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of King George III, sold for £181,600 at Christie's on 8 June 2006; his Portrait of George Douglas, 16th Earl of Morton in the dress of the Royal Company of Archers, sold for £481,250 at Christie's on 5 July 2011; and his portrait of The Dashwood Children sold for $821,000 including premium at Christie's on 29 January 2014. His works are held in many of the world's leading collections, including the Louvre, the Smithsonian Institution, the Royal Collection, the Royal Academy of Arts, the National Portrait Gallery, London, the Tate, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Beechey was granted arms on 16 February 1829.
